novelty.justification: The artifact contains only a research question: "How can component-level performance test results be used to predict system-level performance regressions in microservice-based software systems before the system is fully integrated and deployed?" It provides no concrete technique. The closest Solution Space entries, such as R26 (performance-aware unit tests and regression detection), R15 (model-driven performance engineering for microservices), and R19 (reusing pipeline tests as performance tests), already address closely related component-level performance regression or early performance assessment goals. The artifact's self-reported "novelty_score": 1.0 and "assessment": "high" are not grounded in any comparison against the Solution Space, with "similar_papers_found": 0.
novelty.rubric: Existing: the idea's core method is already clearly present or solved in the Solution Space; only tiny parameter / test-case changes.
novelty.differentiation: No differentiation can be established because the artifact does not propose any method, model, architecture, or mechanism. The high-level goal of linking component/unit-level performance test results to system-level regression prediction already appears in the Solution Space, especially in R26, R15, and R19.

feasibility.justification: The artifact specifies no implementation plan, prediction model, data pipeline, or evaluation workflow. The hypotheses field is empty: "hypotheses_md": "". There is no evidence of a runnable system or even a minimal technical design. From the provided idea alone, a researcher would need to design the entire prediction mechanism, integrate component-level performance data, and build the evaluation harness from scratch, which represents an extreme and undefined engineering burden.
feasibility.rubric: Extreme engineering barrier: requires building complex low-level tooling from scratch (custom compiler plugins, new vulnerability execution sandboxes), or an extremely heavy experimental pipeline with multi-month development.

clarity.justification: The idea is only a task question and an empty hypotheses section. It lacks a defined problem operationalization, proposed method, architecture, experiment design, or evaluation plan. The text gives no concrete technical substance beyond "component-level performance test results" and "system-level performance regressions in microservice-based software systems." This is a vague concept with no actionable plan.
clarity.rubric: Vague concept: full of empty buzzwords; problem undefined; method only gives a high-level direction with little substance.

notes: Scores the intermediate idea artifact (not the final paper).

idea_generation.summary: The artifact provides only the research question plus a self-reported novelty check. It contains no hypothesis, method, model, architecture, or experiment plan; "hypotheses_md" is empty. The claimed high novelty is unsupported and conflicts with existing Solution Space work on performance-aware unit tests and model-driven microservice performance engineering. The proposal is therefore not actionable as stated, with very low clarity and feasibility.
strengths: Identifies a relevant high-level problem: predicting system-level regressions from component-level tests in microservices.
Targets an important cost/time gap between component testing and full-system performance testing.
weaknesses: No concrete method or technical mechanism is proposed.
No experiment design, metrics, baselines, or implementation plan.
Self-reported novelty is not validated against the Solution Space.

original.paper_title: Early Detection of Performance Regressions by Bridging Local Performance Data and Architectural Models

selection.note: mineru key is unreliable; blocks are selected by title/body/inheritance. rescued_from_other counts sections labeled other but treated as typed roles.

claims.statement: The proposed approach can effectively detect end-to-end system performance regressions from local performance deviations with different intensities.
claims.evidence_quote: our approach can effectively detect system performance regressions with different intensities of local performance deviations

claims.statement: The proposed approach can detect regressions as early as the development phase, before full system performance testing is available.
claims.evidence_quote: our approach can detect regressions as early as in the development phase, in contrast to existing approaches that require the system to be fully built and deployed

claims.statement: Significant local performance deviations do not always cause system-level performance regressions, and the approach avoids false alarms in fixed-workload cases without system regressions.
claims.evidence_quote: Our approach does not generate false alarms when there is local performance deviation but no system performance regression.

claims.statement: Under various workloads, the approach maintains effectiveness: TeaStore is consistent with system testing in seven out of nine cases, and TrainTicket model predictions align except for an undetectable L1 case.
claims.evidence_quote: for TeaStore, our approach maintains consistency with the performance testing results in seven out of nine cases

original.overall_conclusion: The proposed approach bridges component-level performance deviation detection and architectural models to infer system-level performance regressions early in the development phase. Across TeaStore and TrainTicket benchmarks, fixed-workload evaluations show that the approach detects most injected regressions while avoiding false alarms in no-regression cases, and various-workload evaluations show maintained consistency in most cases.
original.comparable_notes: The comparison uses open-source systems TeaStore and TrainTicket, injected regressions at L1-L3, Low/Medium/High intensities, component-level tests repeated 30 times, system performance tests run 15 minutes with 5-minute warm-up and repeated 3 times, and regression outcomes derived from response time effect size and CPU MPD differences.

No concrete method components, baselines, ablations, or experimental evidence were provided.
